newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea considers cutting import tax on crude.
newsitem.headline: South Korea considers cutting import tax on crude.

text.p: South Korea is considering cutting the five-percent import tax on crude oil in preparation for energy deregulation, which starts in 1997, a senior government official said on Thursday.

"We're assessing lowering the crude import tax to provide more competitiveness for domestically produced petroleum products against imported products," said Shin Dong-oh, the director general of the petroleum policy division of the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy.
He was speaking at a seminar in Seoul on petroleum policy.
Oil product prices and oil imports and exports will be liberalised from January 1, 1997.
The refining industry will also be liberalised, starting in 1999.

Shin said "In the near future our oil industry must compete against not only local companies but also foreign majors and in order to do that we should get away from expanding capacity but concentrate on cost competitiveness and efficiency."
Shin did not specify how far the import tax on crude might be cut, but said the ministry was holding consultations with other ministries and the industry.
He said cutting costs in production and distribution and improving oil transportation and storage was crucial for the sector's future.
"In order to prepare for the market opening, the refiners who are producers, should form strong ties with distributors and gas stations," he told the seminar.
Separately, Shin said the ministry was looking into increasing the financial support for private companies that are planning overseas oil exploration.
South Korea does not produce any of its own oil, so relies entirely on imports.
